newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Voodoo fighters rout Zaire army in eastern town.
newsitem.headline: Voodoo fighters rout Zaire army in eastern town.

text.p: Zairean rebels using a bizarre mix of child soldiers and voodoo warriors have cut off government forces in an east Zaire town, aid workers said.
The spokesman for the central government in Kinshasa admitted Zaire had been "humiliated" in its war with Rwandan-backed rebels, who have seized more and more towns.
Speaking at a news conference in the capital on Monday, spokesman Boguo Makeli also launched a stinging attack on the international media for "disseminating rebel propaganda".

"The latest discovery of this press is to announce several days in advance that such and such a locality has fallen in the hands of the aggressors, all this with the objective of demoralising our troops and confusing the population," said Boguo, who is Zaire's information minister.
He reaffirmed Zaire's determination to recover a swathe of territory captured by rebels since fighting began in October.
"We must fight to recover the lost territories. We have to first of all settle the military score. We have been attacked, we have been humiliated," Boguo said.
Aid workers said Banyamulenge rebels using Mai-Mai tribal witchcraft fighters, many of them children, cut off army troops in the northeastern town of Bunia on Monday.
"The Banyamulenge have surrounded Bunia with Mai-Mai," said Mustafa Lufungula, local operations head of the Zaire Red Cross in Beni, 140 km (85 miles) from Bunia.
The Banyamulenge are ethnic Tutsis who became the catalyst for a wider rebel insurgency against the Zairean government when they were threatened with expulsion from Zaire in October.

"The Mai-Mai children tell us what is going on, because they trust us, and because we look after them when they are wounded," he added. "The Banyamulenge are using them because of their supposed magic powers, they are taking advantage of them."

The Mai-Mai believe bullets turn into water if their chief has innoculated the target with a secret vaccine. Their army has children as young as 10 years old and their main motive for fighting seems to be loot.
The Mai-Mai take their name from the Swahili word for water and fight in family groups armed with rifles, crossbows, slingshots, spears and home-made shotguns.
Rebels say Bunia, defended by up to 5,000 Zairean troops, is their next target on the northern front as they extend the area they have carved out of eastern Zaire in the past seven weeks.
They say their ultimate aim is to overthrow the central government, already weakened by the prolonged absence of President Mobutu Sese Seko with cancer in Europe.
Boguo did not say how Zaire intended to fight back the rebels given the poor showing of its indisciplined army, but hinted Zaire might be counting on some form of outside help.
"Zaire does not have only enemies, it also has friends," the minister said. He said Zaire was keeping to its transition timetable with elections due next May.
Zairean troops make things easier for the rebels by raping and pillaging as they flee.

Roman Catholic church officials disclosed on Monday how Zairean paratroopers and presidential guards fled advancing rebels after raping elderly nuns and torturing a seminarian at the mission of Our Lady of Peace and a nearby covent about 350 km (220 miles) north of the city of Goma.

The Zairean rebels have also been given a helping hand by the Ugandan army which handed over the Zairean border town of Kasindi after seizing it two weeks ago from Ugandan rebels allegedly backed by Zaire.
